baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Cohen’s move from workers and consumers to a powerful planner retains social history’s attention to class, gender, race and ethnicity.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own BackStory answer on research design explicitly identifies the continuity and change; no assertion that biography replaces social history.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Saving America’s Cities investigates how public redevelopment and residents’ participation changed across postwar cities.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own BackStory discussion of pluralist and participatory democracy, federal resources and community negotiation; urban renewal is assessed with both costs and achievements.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly credits Cohen’s Chicago research while placing greater weight on Prohibition and the election of 1928 in the formation of cross-ethnic political loyalties (2016).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: McGirr’s own answer to the Making a New Deal question. She calls the emphases distinct but not incompatible; this is an acknowledged debt and extension, not a claim that she repudiates Cohen or derives all her work from her.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Brewer uses Cohen’s account of American commodities as symbols of a liberal democratic way of life in his explanation of Cold War consumption.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2010 explicitly credits Cohen alongside de Grazia’s earlier genealogy and other scholarly resources. Cited A Consumers’ Republic(2003) and Citizens and Consumers essay in Daunton/Hilton eds.(2001); neither original read. Specific resource in this historiographical argument, not broad formative influence.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Cites Making a New Deal among studies relating immigrant assimilation to twentieth-century class formation.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, identifies Cohen's 1990 study as an example of the specified historiographical approach, alongside Gerstle and James Barrett. This is a bounded textual reference, not formal mentorship, an exclusive framework or agreement with the whole book. Cohen's original remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Borrows Cohen’s culture-of-unity formulation as a starting point for examining the racial limits of industrial union solidarity.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Sugrue explicitly attributes the phrase to Cohen on391 and cites Making a New Deal in note5 on392. He uses it to frame what racial division eroded and then considers Nelson’s revision. This is a specific conceptual resource rather than unqualified agreement, formal supervision or a claim that every union had achieved unity. Original Cohen book unread; note’s1989 date variant not propagated.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Cohen critiques single-oppression queer politics that obscures race, class and gender hierarchies.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Cohen critiques single-oppression queer politics that obscures race, class and gender hierarchies.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The teaching source presents Cohen’s intervention within intersectional analysis; the target is this specific debate, not all queer or sexuality history.

claim_projection.subject: work:cohen_queer_1997
claim_projection.note: Qualified teaching view; read the exact claim endpoints and evidence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Against Cohen's technological determinism: the 'material base' is social and historical, and the separation of the economic from the political is specific to capitalism (1981)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Verso repost of NLR I/127 (read in part): Cohen's book is used 'to support an argument against a social interpretation of materialism'; 'what Cohen's technological determinism does is to repeat the error of the political economists: he generalizes the particular historical experience of capitalism'. Callinicos (1990, read): this 'is by no means the first time that Wood has used Brenner's work to distinguish her alternative reading of historical materialism from Cohen's' (p. 111). Brenner (2016): 'Here Ellen's main target was … Gerald Cohen'.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The Rule of Freedom (2003): the liberal governance of the nineteenth-century city 'depended on the "rule of freedom"', read through 'maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' in London and Manchester
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Verso description (read 2026-10-22): 'The liberal governance of the nineteenth-century state and city depended on the "rule of freedom"'; the city's 'layout, architecture, infrastructure' and 'such artifacts as maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' examined for 'the impersonal, often invisible forms of social direction and control built into the infrastructure of modern life'. The body is unread; Cohen (AHR 2004) and Frohman (CJH 2004) are metadata only. Moderate: a publisher's statement of the book's argument.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: 'The digital revolution has created endless opportunities via blogs, websites, YouTube, and social media' for the historian's stories (2013); presidential columns 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' and 'Scholarly Authority in a Wikified World' (2012); 'digital scholarship' named among his fields
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Moderate. The 2013 sentence is read (open AHA text, data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3); the 2012 Perspectives columns are known by title from the CV (p. 8) and his AHA-writings page; the CV (p. 1) lists 'digital scholarship' among his fields and (p. 10) the websites he built. The columns themselves are unread. No target strand: the entry's strands are per-work; the coordinator may attach it to the 2005 Cohen–Rosenzweig strand or leave it unattached.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Defines cultural history through historically situated meanings, conflicting desires and unintended consequences.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Author answers in the Cohen interview, section II; Serlin interview answers on overlapping chance/control. These are Lears’s stated interpretive methods, not certification of each example or a field-wide consensus.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Connects commercial persuasion to culturally specific practices of confidence, trust and uncertainty.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cohen interview, section I, where Lears discusses Fables of Abundance and the historical settings of confidence. The complete advertising monograph remains unread and no timeless national character is inferred.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Lears invokes Thompson’s unintended-consequences formulation and his account of law’s relative autonomy when explaining cultural meaning and power.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Cohen answer expressly paraphrases Thompson, without establishing the original aphorism’s exact wording or source. Own1985p590uses Whigs and Hunters1975pp258–269 among plural models for ideology’s promise. Specific resources, not a claim to adopt all Thompson.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Questions the limits of Higham’s nativism framework and its economic-downturn explanation of restriction.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, appreciates the classic account while arguing that legislative triumph narratives can obscure categories produced after enactment. The 2024 article treats eugenics as one cause and argues that nativist surges accompany structural change even during expansion, rather than simply cyclical downturns. Benton-Cohen retains credit for the Dillingham finding. This does not certify every historical example or refute Higham's entire work; the original books remain unread.
